paper_title: RLSplat: Resource-Linear Budget Control for Feed-forward 3D Gaussian Splatting

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Feed-forward 3D Gaussian Splatting (FF3DGS) reconstructs 3D scenes from images in a single forward pass, making it well-suited to applications that must operate within limited resource budgets. To further improve its practicality, recent budget-controllable FF3DGS methods allow the number of Gaussians to be adjusted at inference, so that the output meets a given storage limit or rendering-latency constraint. However, these methods overlook the cost of inference itself: to produce a representation with the target number of Gaussians, they first predict a dense set of Gaussians and then prune or select from it, requiring nearly constant latency and peak memory regardless of the budget. We therefore propose RLSplat, a resource-linear budget-controllable FF3DGS framework whose representation size, inference latency, and peak memory all decrease linearly as the Gaussian budget is reduced. Instead of pruning or selection, RLSplat learns a Gaussian allocation policy that distributes the budget across local scene regions, so that exactly the requested number of Gaussians is generated. These Gaussians are then refined through resource-linear Gaussian decoding, in which each Gaussian attends only to nearby Gaussians found via an efficient hierarchical neighbor search, so that the decoding cost decreases linearly with fewer Gaussians. In zero-shot evaluation, RLSplat outperforms prior budget-controllable methods at every budget, surpassing the strongest baseline even with 4$\times$ fewer Gaussians, while running up to 4.1$\times$ faster with 9.6$\times$ less peak memory at low budgets.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) (Kerbl et al., 2023) has become leading representation for photorealistic, real-time novel view synthesis, supporting applications from AR/VR (Qian et al., 2024; Jiang et al., 2024) to robotics (Keetha et al., 2024; Matsuki et al., 2024) and digital content creation (Tang et al., 2024; Chen et al., 2024b). Its explicit form further allows it to serve as 3D scene representation for downstream models, such as 3D vision-language models (Li et al., 2025; Thai et al., 2025). Since per-scene optimization of 3DGS takes minutes to hours and requires many calibrated views, feed-forward 3DGS (FF3DGS) methods instead predict Gaussians in single forward pass (Charatan et al., 2024; Chen et al., 2024a), and recent variants even operate directly on uncalibrated images (Jiang et al., 2025). Owing to this fast and readily available reconstruction, FF3DGS has become practical choice for applications that build 3D scene representations on the fly. Corresponding author. Preprint. Figure 1: Budget-controllable quality, memory, and latency trade-offs. (a) RLSplat achieves the highest PSNR across the evaluated total Gaussian budgets B. (b) At the 2K budget, RLSplat uses 9.6 less peak VRAM than F4Splat while attaining higher PSNR. (c) As is reduced, RLSplats inference latency decreases approximately linearly, whereas the latencies of F4Splat and EcoSplat remain nearly constant. In axis tick labels, 1K = 1,024. . Early FF3DGS methods (Charatan et al., 2024; Chen et al., 2024a; Ye et al., 2025) simplify the problem by allocating fixed number of Gaussians to each input pixel, which allows the feed-forward network to be trained effectively. However, this pixel-aligned design produces many redundant Gaussians, since Gaussians from overlapping views become increasingly redundant as more views are added. To address this redundancy, query-based methods (An et al., 2026; Itkin et al., 2026) decode fixed set of learnable query tokens into Gaussians. Yet neither approach can adjust the number of Gaussians without retraining. This lack of controllability makes it difficult to adapt to the diverse resource budgets encountered in real-world deployment. To address this, recent works have proposed Gaussian budget-controllable methods. Given Gaussian budget B, EcoSplat (Park et al., 2026) first predicts one Gaussian per pixel and keeps the Gaussians with the highest opacity. F4Splat (Kim et al., 2026) instead predicts Gaussians at multiple scales and selects the Gaussians. However, these methods overlook the computational cost of inference itself. Both methods first predict much larger set of candidate Gaussians before reducing them to B, so their inference latency and peak memory remain nearly constant regardless of the budget, as shown in Fig. 1(b) and (c). We therefore propose RLSplat, budget-controllable FF3DGS framework that is resource-linear: both its representation size and inference cost scale linearly with the budget B. Given uncalibrated images and budget B, geometry backbone encodes the images into anchor tokens, each representing local 3D region of the scene. To obtain compact representation, we formulate Gaussian generation as an allocation problem rather than pruning or selection: we predict how many Gaussians to assign to each anchors region, summing to B. Since these discrete allocations are non-differentiable and can only be evaluated by rendering the resulting Gaussians, we model this prediction as Gaussian allocation policy and train it with policy optimization, using Group Sequence Policy Optimization (GSPO) (Zheng et al., 2025) with rendering quality as the reward. Given the allocation, each anchor token spawns as many Gaussian tokens as its allocated count, yielding total of Gaussian tokens. To efficiently decode these tokens into the final Gaussians, we introduce resource-linear decoder. It refines each Gaussian token through local cross-attention over its Kgs nearest Gaussian tokens, which we find with an efficient hierarchical neighbor search. Whereas global self-attention over all tokens costs O(B2), each token here attends to only Kgs neighbors, so the decoding cost is O(BKgs) and scales linearly with the Gaussian budget (Fig. 1(c)). As result, RLSplat achieves higher quality than prior budget-controllable methods at every budget (Fig. 1(a)), while its peak memory and latency decrease with the budget. At 2K Gaussians, it achieves higher PSNR than F4Splat while using 9.6 less peak memory (Fig. 1(b)) and running 4.1 faster (Fig. 1(c)). In summary, our contributions are as follows: We identify that existing budget-controllable FF3DGS methods control only the size of the output, not the cost of producing it, and introduce RLSplat, resource-linear FF3DGS framework in which the number of Gaussians, inference latency, and peak memory all decrease linearly as the budget is reduced. 2 We formulate Gaussian generation as an allocation problem and learn Gaussian allocation policy via policy optimization that places exactly Gaussians where the scene needs them, together with resource-linear decoder whose cost decreases linearly as the budget decreases through local cross-attention and an efficient hierarchical neighbor search. RLSplat consistently outperforms prior budget-controllable methods across all budgets. At budget of 2K Gaussians, it improves PSNR by 0.9 dB over F4Splat while using 9.6 less peak memory and running 4.1 faster.

sections.title: 2 Related Work
sections.content: Feed-Forward 3D Gaussian Splatting. 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) (Kerbl et al., 2023) represents scene with explicit Gaussian primitives and achieves real-time rendering, but requires timeconsuming per-scene optimization from many calibrated views. Feed-forward 3DGS (FF3DGS) methods instead predict Gaussians in single forward pass, from single image (Szymanowicz et al., 2024) or from few posed views (Charatan et al., 2024; Chen et al., 2024a; Xu et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2024). Building on 3D foundation models (Wang et al., 2024; Leroy et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2025), recent methods further remove the need for known camera poses (Ye et al., 2025; Smart et al., 2024; Huang & Mikolajczyk, 2025; Jiang et al., 2025). Most of these methods predict one Gaussian per pixel or per voxel, so the number of Gaussians is determined by the input resolution and the number of views rather than by the scene content. This leads to redundant Gaussians in overlapping and textureless regions, and the number of Gaussians cannot be specified directly. Compact and Gaussian budget-controllable FF3DGS. For per-scene 3DGS, many works aim to represent scene with fewer Gaussians without sacrificing quality, either by pruning redundant Gaussians (Fan et al., 2024; Lee et al., 2024; Papantonakis et al., 2024) or by deciding where to place Gaussians under fixed or constrained budget during densification (Fang & Wang, 2024; Mallick et al., 2024; Kheradmand et al., 2024). These methods, however, rely on iterative per-scene optimization. In FF3DGS, C3G (An et al., 2026) and GlobalSplat (Itkin et al., 2026) decode fixed set of learnable query tokens into compact sets of Gaussians, whose size is determined by the architecture. EcoSplat (Park et al., 2026) and F4Splat (Kim et al., 2026) instead accept target count at inference, by keeping the Gaussians with the highest budget-conditioned opacity and by selecting one of multiple scales per region, respectively; both derive the output from dense set of candidates. ZipSplat (Veicht et al., 2026), developed concurrently with our work, controls the number of Gaussians by clustering visual tokens at inference. In contrast, we learn to allocate exactly the requested number of Gaussians and decode only those, so that our inference cost scales with the budget. Policy optimization. Policy gradient methods (Williams, 1992; Schulman et al., 2017) optimize non-differentiable, discrete decisions from scalar reward, and have been applied to generative vision models, e.g., to align diffusion models with reward functions (Black et al., 2024). Grouprelative variants such as GRPO (Shao et al., 2024) and GSPO (Zheng et al., 2025) remove the need for learned value function by normalizing rewards within group of samples, and have become standard for fine-tuning large language models. In particular, GSPO defines the importance ratio from the likelihood of the whole sequence rather than of individual tokens, and clips it at the sequence level. We adopt this approach to learn Gaussian allocation, treating an allocation as sequence of Gaussians and using rendering quality as the reward.

sections.title: 3 Method
sections.content: We present RLSplat, feed-forward 3DGS framework whose Gaussian count and inference cost are both controlled by single budget B. Rather than pruning or selecting from dense set of Gaussians, RLSplat formulates Gaussian generation as allocation: Gaussian allocation policy decides how many Gaussians each local region of the scene receives (Sec. 3.2), and resource-linear decoder generates the allocated Gaussians and efficiently refines them with local cross-attention (Sec. 3.3). We begin with an overview (Sec. 3.1) and conclude with the training procedure (Sec. 3.4). 3 Figure 2: Overview of RLSplat. Objectives. To supervise view synthesis, we apply reconstruction loss Lrecon, combining pixelwise MSE and LPIPS between the rendered and ground-truth target views. For geometric alignment, camera loss Lcam supervises the translation, rotation, and field-of-view of the predicted context cameras. Additionally, projection loss Lproj reprojects each anchors Gaussians toward their source image patch. Incorporating cheirality penalty to prevent Gaussians from landing behind the camera, Lproj effectively ties an anchors allocation to specific scene region and prevents arbitrary drift. These terms are combined with the locality regularizers (Lvor and Loffset) previously introduced in Sec. 3.3. Finally, during the policy training stage, we activate the policy loss Lpolicy = Jpolicy (Eq. (4)) to optimize the discrete allocations via GSPO. The overall training objectives are detailed in Sec. E. Two-stage training. We train RLSplat in two stages. In base training, we train the encoder and decoder with random allocations, and sample budgets over the full supported range. This exposes the decoder to widely varying per-anchor counts, so that it learns to render diverse allocations before the policy is introduced. In policy training, we add the policy head, initialized to output uniform probabilities (Sec. B), and fine-tune the entire model with the policy loss Lpolicy. Since base training involves no policy, there is no reference policy to regularize toward, and unlike typical RL finetuning, we do not apply KL penalty. During this stage, budgets are sampled with skew toward the lower end of the range, where the choice of allocation matters most for rendering quality.

sections.title: 4 Experiments
sections.content: Datasets and evaluation. We train on RealEstate10K (RE10K) (Zhou et al., 2018) with {2, 3, 4, 6, 8, 12, 24} uncalibrated context views. To assess generalization, we evaluate the RE10Ktrained model zero-shot on ACID (Liu et al., 2021) (249 test scenes), which consists of aerial footage of coastal and natural scenes. We follow the evaluation protocol of F4Splat (Kim et al., 2026) at resolution of 256 256 and report PSNR, SSIM, and LPIPS together with the number of Gaussians (#GS). To measure inference cost, we report the latency and peak VRAM of Gaussian generation, excluding data loading, pose alignment, and rendering. All methods are run on single RTX A6000 with batch size of one. For each budget, we discard the first scene as warm-up, reset the peakmemory counter before each timed run, and report the mean over the test scenes. Baselines. We mainly compare with budget-controllable methods, EcoSplat (Park et al., 2026) and F4Splat (Kim et al., 2026), which take target Gaussian count as input at inference time. We evaluate all methods at the same requested Gaussian budgets, with particular focus on the low-budget regime. For broader comparison, we also include budget-fixed methods, which place Gaussians uniformly, either one per pixel (NoPoSplat (Ye et al., 2025), SPFSplat (Huang & Mikolajczyk, 2025)) or one per voxel (AnySplat (Jiang et al., 2025)). Their Gaussian count is therefore determined by the input resolution and the number of views, or by the voxel size, rather than chosen by the user. 6 Table 1: Budget-controllable methods on ACID (zero-shot from RE10K). In the base training stage, we train the geometry backbone and Gaussian decoder with random allocations for 40,000 steps. In the subsequent policy training stage, we train for an additional 5,000 steps. During training, the Gaussian budget is sampled from [2048, 16384V ], where is the number of input views. Unless otherwise noted, we use Kanc=Kgs=16 for Gaussian decoding in all experiments. Details are provided in Secs. and F. 4.1 Novel-view Synthesis Results Table 1 compares RLSplat with budget-controllable methods at matched budgets of 1K, 2K, and 4K Gaussians per context view. RLSplat achieves the best LPIPS, SSIM, and PSNR at every budget and view count. Importantly, its advantage becomes increasingly pronounced as the Gaussian budget decreases. For example, with 8 context views, the PSNR advantage over F4Splat grows from 0.74 dB at 4K Gaussians per view to 0.99 dB at 2K and 1.22 dB at 1K. This trend is consistent across 16 and 24 context views, demonstrating that RLSplat preserves reconstruction quality particularly well under tight representation budgets. This robustness is consistent with how the final Gaussians are decoded: the baselines predict dense set of Gaussians and then prune or select from it, whereas RLSplat directly decodes the requested number of Gaussians and refines them through resourcelinear decoding. For broader comparison, Table 2 includes budget-fixed methods whose output size is determined by the input. Despite using substantially fewer Gaussians, RLSplat outperforms all of these methods on LPIPS, SSIM, and PSNR across all view counts. In particular, with 24 context views, RLSplat achieves 25.58 dB PSNR using only 24K Gaussians, compared with 25.00 dB for SPFSplat using 1536K Gaussians, corresponding to 64 fewer Gaussians. Fig. 4 shows how each method uses the same total budget of 8K Gaussians on RE10K. In the highlighted stair region, EcoSplat and F4Splat retain 2,521 and 3,026 Gaussians, respectively, whereas RLSplat allocates 5,388 Gaussians to the thin, high-frequency structure. The tile-wise allocation maps further show that RLSplat concentrates its budget around the stair balusters while spending fewer Gaussians on the comparatively smooth wall. This targeted allocation leads to substantially better reconstruction of the thin structures: the local PSNR of the highlighted region increases from 17.79 dB for EcoSplat and 20.00 dB for F4Splat to 23.51 dB for RLSplat . The improvement is also reflected in the full-view PSNR (21.82, 23.42, and 26.51 dB, respectively). These results illustrate 7 Figure 4: Qualitative comparison under the same Gaussian budget. All methods use 8K Gaussians on RE10K. For each method, we show the rendered view and PSNR, zoomed region and its local PSNR, the Gaussian centers in the highlighted region (red), and 1616 tile-wise map of the number of Gaussians. RLSplat places more Gaussians around the thin stair balusters (5,388 vs. 3,026 for F4Splat and 2,521 for EcoSplat), preserving the fine structure that the baselines blur. that the learned allocation policy uses fixed Gaussian budget more effectively by concentrating capacity where fine geometric and appearance details require it. 4.2 Ablation Studies and Analysis Unless otherwise noted, all experiments in this section are evaluated on ACID with 8 views at total budget of B=8,192 (1,024 Gaussians per view). Fig. 7 varies the number of neighbors Kgs at inference while keeping Kanc fixed. For every Kgs, peak VRAM decreases linearly with B, and larger Kgs improves quality at the cost of memory. As the budget grows, the quality gap between different Kgs narrows, while the memory cost of larger Kgs increases. Since Kgs can be changed without retraining, users can choose smaller value at large budgets to save memory with little loss in quality, and larger Kgs at small budgets where it matters most. sections.title: 5 Conclusion
sections.content: Figure 7: Gaussian-neighbor ablation. Kgs is varied at inference with single trained model; Kanc=16 is fixed. We presented RLSplat, budget-controllable feed-forward 3DGS framework whose inference cost scales linearly with the requested number of Gaussians B. Gaussian allocation policy, trained with GSPO, distributes exactly Gaussians across anchors, and resource-linear decoder refines them through local cross-attention with hierarchical neighbor search. On ACID, RLSplat achieves the best rendering quality among budget-controllable methods at every tested budget. Its latency and peak memory decrease linearly with B, and it matches or exceeds the quality of the baselines at fraction of their memory and latency.

sections.title: A Limitations and Future Work
sections.content: Image encoding remains fixed cost independent of B, which bounds the achievable speed-up at small budgets. We also evaluate at resolution of 256 256 and in single cross-dataset setting. RLSplat controls both the size of the representation and the cost of producing it. It can therefore serve as 3D scene representation for downstream tasks that have their own resource limits, such as 3D vision-language models and robot learning. Evaluating it on such tasks is natural next step.

sections.title: B Allocation Policy Details
sections.content: Policy head. The policy head predicts logit ln for each anchor token, and the allocation probabilities are obtained as = softmax(l) with = {ln}N n=1. The head is LN(d) Linear(d, h) SiLU Linear(h, 1), applied per anchor token. The last linear layer is zero-initialized, so starts uniform. Budget conditioning. The head is modulated by FiLM parameters (γ, η). They are predicted from single scalar, the log-ratio of the requested budget to the number of anchors, = log2(B/N ), by Linear(1, h) SiLU Linear(h, 2d). The modulation is applied after the layer norm: hidden hidden (cid:0)1 + tanh γ(u)(cid:1) + η(u). The last layer of the FiLM generator is also zero-initialized. The ratio B/N is floored at 1/64 so that stays finite for very small budgets. Policy initialization at the start of policy training. The policy head does not exist during base training. It is created with zero-initialized output layers when policy training begins, so it outputs exactly 0 for every anchor and is uniform at the first policy-training step. Base trainings random allocation already covers this regime, so the transition introduces no distribution shift for the decoder. Deterministic integer allocation. At inference, and for the reconstruction loss during policy training, the expected counts Bp are converted into an integer allocation by systematic rounding with fixed phase. Anchors are laid out on line in fixed (view, patch-raster) order, anchor owning the interval [BPn1, BPn) with Pn = (cid:80) mn pm and P0 = 0. We place points at φ, φ + 1, . . . , φ + 1 with φ = 1 2 and count those that fall inside each interval: 2 = (cid:6)BPn φ(cid:7) (cid:6)BPn1 φ(cid:7). This rule has three properties we rely on: (i) the counts sum to exactly B, since the telescoping sum equals 1 2 = B; (ii) every count is either Bpn or Bpn, since an interval of length Bpn contains that many unit-spaced points; and (iii) an anchor with pn = 0 receives no Gaussian. With uniformly random phase, Eq. (11) is systematic resampling and satisfies E[kn] = Bpn, the mean of the multinomial rollouts. Fixing φ makes it deterministic. It needs single cumulative sum, so it takes O(N ) time, involves no sorting and has no ties to break. We compute it in double precision and renormalize PN to one. (11)

sections.title: C GSPO Training Details
sections.content: GSPO hyperparameters. Table 6 ablates the two hyperparameters of the rollouts: the group size and the rollout temperature τ . With τ = 1, the rollouts are drawn from the tempered proposal rather than from p, and the ratio is no longer one. The policy is robust to both hyperparameters: all settings are within 0.11 dB PSNR of each other. = 5 performs best, and τ = 1.0, which samples from the policy itself, outperforms both tempered variants. We use = 5 and τ = 1.0 throughout. Settled hyperparameters. Policy training uses = 5 rollouts and policy loss weight λpolicy = 1.0; the entropy and KL weights are both 0, and no minimum per-anchor count is enforced. Base training (Sec. 3.4) trains the encoder and decoder without an allocation head at all, so there is no pretrained policy to serve as KL reference at the start of policy training. sections.title: D Decoder Details
sections.content: Gaussian token construction. For anchor with kn allocated Gaussians, token {0, . . . , kn 1} has relative position ρn,r = (r + 1 2 )/kn (0, 1), so the tokens of any anchor tile the unit interval regardless of kn. We use mip-NeRF-style (Barron et al., 2021) integrated positional encoding PE(ρ, k) that averages Fourier features over the tokens bin of width 1/kn, which suppresses the frequencies that would otherwise alias between nearby values of kn. The token is (cid:1)MLP(cid:0)PE(ρn,r, kn)(cid:1)+βn, (αn, βn) = Linear(cid:0)LN(an)(cid:1), (12) n,r = an +(cid:0)1+tanh αn t0 with the FiLM layer zero-initialized. All tokens across batch are packed into one sequence, so no computation is spent on padding. Neighbor search. Anchor centroids µn are the mean initial centers of each anchors tokens. anc(n), the Kanc=16 nearest anchors to (including itself), is found once by K-nearestneighbor search over the detached centroids and shared by all = 2 decoder layers. Gaussians neighbor set gs(b) is the Kgs nearest Gaussian tokens, by detached Euclidean distance, among the tokens belonging to anc(nb). Residual head. The initial-Gaussian head and the residual head share the same architecture, LN Linear(d, 256) SiLU Linear(256, 11+3dsh), predicting center offset (3), an opacity logit (1), scales (3), quaternion (4), and spherical-harmonic color coefficients. The residual head is zero-initialized, and its center output is scaled by αµ.

sections.title: E Training Details
sections.content: Context views are loaded at 256 256 and bilinearly upsampled to 504 504 immediately before the backbone, while target views, losses, and evaluation remain at 256 256. The DVLT (Burzio et al., 2026) backbone runs 12 inference steps. Each training step draws the number of context views from the divisors of 24, {2, 3, 4, 6, 8, 12, 24}, and sets the batch size to 24/V , so that every step processes 24 context views in total regardless of . Base training. The encoder and decoder are trained for 40K steps with allocations drawn uniformly at random, which exposes the decoder to wide range of per-anchor counts before any policy is learned. The per-sample budget is sampled from Beta distribution over [2048, 16384V ]. We use AdamW with learning rate of 104 (0.1 for the backbone), 1,000 warm-up steps, and cosine decay on 4 GPUs. The loss weights are 1.0 for MSE, 0.05 for VGG-LPIPS, 0.1 for the reprojection term and 0.05 for the cheirality term of Lproj, and 1.0 for Lvor. The offset loss Loffset is weighted λoffset = 0.01. Policy training. Starting from the pretrained model, all parameters are fine-tuned for 5K steps with = 5 rollouts per step and rollout temperature of τ = 1.0; the render used for the reconstruction loss is produced from the deterministic allocation of Sec. 3.2. The learning rate is reduced to 105, with 30 multiplier on the allocation head, and Loffset is disabled. The policy loss Lpolicy is weighted 1.0. Each samples budget is drawn independently from Beta(1, 4) over the same range, which biases training toward low budgets where allocation matters most. The total budget of step is capped, so that peak memory is bounded independently of the per-sample maximum.

sections.title: F Ablation Protocol
sections.content: Each ablation changes single component relative to its reference, except for the variant that removes both locality regularizers. Pretraining ablations  (Table 3)  are trained from scratch for 5K steps, one eighth of the full schedule, with all step-dependent schedules (cosine horizon, optimizer warm-up, view-sampler warm-up, and validation and checkpoint intervals) scaled by the same factor. We compare the full recipe with variants that remove the local refinement module, the projection loss (both its reprojection and cheirality terms), the offset loss, or both the offset and Voronoi losses. The neighbor match rate without the Voronoi loss is measured with the same schedule. Allocation ablations (Tables 4 and 6) fine-tune for 1K steps from single shared pretrained checkpoint and vary the group size {3, 5, 7}, the temperature τ {0.8, 1.0, 1.2}, and the allocation rule, replacing the learned policy with uniform split or learning-free Sobel-energy heuristic. Since shorter run anneals on its own cosine schedule, each variant is trained for its own horizon rather than truncated from longer run. All ablations are evaluated on ACID with 8 context views (249 scenes). Allocation ablations are evaluated at B/V = 1024.

sections.title: G Allocation Policy Visualizations
sections.content: Figs. 8 to 10 extend Fig. 6 to twelve RE10K two-view test scenes, all at an average of 1024 Gaussians per view. For each anchor we show its expected allocation relative to uniform split, pnN , where is the number of anchors over both views; 1 corresponds to about 0.8 Gaussians per anchor at this budget. This is the policys output before the budget is rounded to integer counts. The corner label is the fraction of the total budget that goes to that view. We show the raw per-anchor maps next to the smoothed maps used in the main paper (Gaussian filter, σ=1 anchor, applied to log2 of the map), so the smoothing can be checked for artifacts: it only removes anchor-level noise and leaves the spatial pattern unchanged.

sections.title: H Additional Qualitative Comparison
sections.content: Figs. 11 to 13 compare RLSplat with F4Splat and EcoSplat as the Gaussian budget is reduced from 128K to 32K. As the budget decreases, the baselines progressively blur or lose thin, high-frequency structures such as stair balusters, railings, window frames, and foliage, while RLSplat retains these details at every budget. This is consistent with Table 1, where RLSplat exhibits substantially less quality degradation than the baselines as the budget decreases. Unlike the baselines, which reduce dense set of candidates, RLSplat allocates the budget where the scene needs it and decodes only those Gaussians, preserving fine details even under the tightest budgets. 15 Figure 8: More allocation policies (1/3). Raw (left pair) and smoothed (right pair) allocation maps on log scale (0.25 to 4; red: more, blue: fewer). In these indoor scenes the policy shifts budget toward the view with more structure and away from near-blank walls and doorways. 16 Figure 9: More allocation policies (2/3). Same layout as Fig. 8. Budget moves away from dark or under-exposed regions, such as the arch frame and the darkened hillside, and concentrates on the lit part of the scene or on the object. Figure 10: More allocation policies (3/3). Same layout as Fig. 8. When the two views are nearly identical, the budget stays close to an even split between them, and the policy acts within each view instead: it empties water and sky and spends the budget on buildings, vegetation and shorelines. 18 Figure 11: Qualitative comparison across Gaussian budgets (1/3). 19 Figure 12: Qualitative comparison across Gaussian budgets (2/3).
